notes: Permission to appeal against strike-out of s.459 petition; Neuberger LJ refused application on clear no-prospect grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Permission refused to appeal strike-out of unfair prejudice petition
key_facts: Mr Branch applied in person for permission to appeal against David Richards J's strike-out of his section 459 petition relating to Oasis (Poole) Management Ltd, a company limited by guarantee of flat owners.
The petition alleged unfair prejudice arising from company expenditure and conduct including allegations of anti-Semitism among fellow shareholders in a block of flats.
The judge held Mr Branch could not demonstrate unfair prejudice distinct from ordinary shareholder disappointment and that the petition had no reasonable prospect of success.
Mr Branch challenged the authenticity of the judgment, section 310's effect, and whether he suffered unfair prejudice from being out of pocket like other shareholders.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against strike-out of an unfair prejudice petition.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; strike-out upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a section 459 petition has been properly struck out as having no reasonable prospect of success, permission to appeal should be refused unless there is some real prospect of reversal; being out of pocket in the same way as other shareholders in a residents' management company does not amount to unfair prejudice, and section 310 does not assist a shareholder seeking relief on these facts.
legal_issues: Whether there was any prospect of overturning the strike-out of the section 459 petition
Meaning of unfair prejudice in a flat-owners' management company
Effect of section 310 Companies Act 1985 on shareholder petitions
Whether alleged defects in the judgment undermined the strike-out order

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment with clear refusal and reasoning on unfair prejudice and strike-out principles.

notes: Security for costs against illiquid BVI claimant; Park J ordered payment despite subsidiary undertaking.

enrichment.short_title: Security for costs against illiquid BVI claimant challenging solicitor fees
key_facts: Longstaff International Ltd, a BVI company managed in Jersey, sued Baker McKenzie for repayment of about £750,000 in professional fees said to have been paid by mistake.
Longstaff's main asset was shares in Redwell Ltd, whose Isle of Dogs development site was valued at £12m, but both companies were substantially illiquid with large net current liabilities.
Baker McKenzie applied for security for costs relying on Longstaff's lack of liquidity rather than its non-resident status.
Redwell offered an undertaking to meet any costs liability of Longstaff, but without payment into court or bank guarantee.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Opposed application for security for costs in Chancery proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Security for costs ordered in the modest amount requested; security to be by payment into court, acceptable bank guarantee, or other form accepted by the defendant, failing which the claim would be dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 25.13(2)(c) is satisfied where a claimant company could not pay the defendant's costs when they fall due despite positive net assets, because illiquid fixed assets do not remove the condition; a subsidiary's unsecured undertaking does not take the claimant outside paragraph (c) and is not acceptable security where enforcement would depend on hostile directors negotiating future bank finance.
legal_issues: Whether Longstaff came within CPR 25.13(2)(a) as resident out of the jurisdiction
Whether CPR 25.13(2)(c) applied given illiquidity despite asset value
Whether Redwell's undertaking provided adequate security
Whether it was just to order security and in what form

notes: Unfair dismissal capability appeal; Court of Appeal restored ET finding that employer acted reasonably.

enrichment.short_title: Housing manager's capability dismissal after refusal of occupational health consent
key_facts: Ms O'Donoghue, a housing manager for Elmbridge Housing Trust, was off work from March 2001 with stress or depression and refused direct communication, dealing only through her union representative.

The Trust repeatedly requested completion of occupational health consent forms to obtain medical advice; she partially completed forms but deleted consent for disclosure to the employer and later refused to sign revised forms properly.
She was dismissed for incapability on 28 June 2001 after extended deadlines; the Employment Tribunal found the dismissal fair.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal set aside that decision as perverse and substituted a finding of unfair dismissal for misconduct, but the Court of Appeal restored the ET decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision allowing an appeal from an Employment Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Employment Tribunal decision restored; dismissal held fair; respondent ordered to pay appellant's costs assessed at £10,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employer dismissed for incapability after prolonged sickness absence because an employee would not give effective consent for occupational health information despite repeated reasonable requests, the ET's conclusion that dismissal was within the range of reasonable responses was not perverse; the EAT erred in treating the reason as misconduct and in substituting its own decision rather than remitting the case.
legal_issues: Whether the ET decision was perverse or insufficiently reasoned
Whether dismissal was for capability or conduct
Whether the employee had effectively consented to medical disclosure
Effect of failure to complete internal appeal procedure on fairness

notes: Diving injury appeal; Occupiers Liability Act 1984 duty not established for hidden underwater obstruction.

enrichment.short_title: Diving injury at gravel pit: no occupiers' duty for hidden underwater obstruction
key_facts: The appellant, aged almost 20, ran into Astbury Mere and dived into shallow water despite 'no swimming' notices, striking his head on a fibreglass container on the lake bed covered in silt.
Astbury Water Park Ltd and Maxout Ltd held licence rights over the mere used for fishing, sailing and other water sports adjacent to a country park.
Morland J held the defendants were occupiers but owed no duty regarding the obvious risk of diving into shallow water and dismissed the claim.
The container was not found until an underwater search in 2002; evidence showed it was not visible from the surface even when its location was known.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of a personal injury claim.
enrichment.ratio: Unlike Tomlinson, injury here was caused by the state of the premises, but section 1(3)(a) of the Occupiers Liability Act 1984 was not satisfied because the occupiers were not aware of the obstruction and the claimant failed to prove they had reasonable grounds to believe it existed; there was no obligation to carry out underwater inspection of the lake bed.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant was a visitor under the 1957 Act or a non-visitor under the 1984 Act
Whether injury was due to the state of the premises
Whether section 1(3) conditions for a duty to non-visitors were met
Whether occupiers should have inspected the shallow area for obstructions

Donoghue v Folkestone Properties Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 231

confidence.notes: Clear Tomlinson distinction and section 1(3)(a) analysis with reliable witness evidence on visibility.

notes: Unfair dismissal preliminary issue; internal appeal demotion revived contract before ET hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Chef's unfair dismissal claim fails where appeal substituted demotion for dismissal
key_facts: Mr Roberts, a long-serving train chef, was dismissed for misconduct on 6 November 2001 after a disciplinary hearing relating to alleged complicity in theft of catering stock.
He appealed and lodged an ET1 for unfair dismissal on 5 February 2002 before the appeal was heard.
On 6 February 2002 the internal appeal reduced dismissal to demotion to Customer Service Assistant and treated the intervening period as suspension without pay.
Mr Roberts never returned to work and was later treated as having resigned; the ET held he had not been dismissed and the EAT dismissed his appeal on a point of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on whether the claimant was dismissed for purposes of an unfair dismissal claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Employment Tribunal and EAT decisions upheld; no dismissal found after successful contractual appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a contract provides for disciplinary appeal and the employee invokes it, a successful appeal substituting demotion for dismissal revives the existing contract with retrospective effect; filing ET proceedings while still dismissed but before the appeal outcome does not freeze jurisdiction or establish that a dismissal occurred for the purposes of the claim.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Roberts remained dismissed after the internal appeal decision
Whether ET proceedings issued before appeal outcome established jurisdiction
Whether demotion amounted to re-engagement on a new contract
Application of contractual disciplinary appeal procedures

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural chronology and clear ratio on Savage/Tipton principles.

notes: Metallgesellschaft GLO test case; Park J held premature ACT compensation uses compound interest.

enrichment.short_title: Metallgesellschaft ACT compensation: compound interest on premature tax payments
key_facts: Sempra Metals Ltd (formerly Metallgesellschaft Ltd), a UK subsidiary of a German parent, paid advance corporation tax on dividends when denied group income elections available to UK-parent groups.
Following the ECJ decision in Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst, Sempra sought restitution for timing disadvantage over periods between ACT payment and set-off against mainstream corporation tax.
The case was a group litigation order test case on whether compensation should use compound or simple interest.
Sempra also claimed post-utilisation interest from accrual of the cause of action until judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Group litigation test case in the Chancery Division determining principles of quantum for EC-law ACT restitution claims.
enrichment.outcome: Restitution or compensation for the premature tax payment period to be calculated using compound interest at a conventional market rate; post-utilisation interest under section 35A limited to simple interest.
enrichment.ratio: Community law requires full restitution for prematurely paid ACT, which only compound interest over the premature tax payment period can achieve; English restrictions on standalone interest claims cannot limit that primary loss, but section 35A governs ancillary post-judgment interest and permits only simple interest.
legal_issues: Compound versus simple interest for premature ACT payments
Conventional versus actual loss measurement
Distinction between primary EC-law loss and ancillary domestic interest
Treatment of utilised versus unutilised ACT

notes: Environmental Protection Act abatement notice appeals; procedural rulings on withdrawal and no-case submission.

enrichment.short_title: Motorcycle noise abatement notice appeals: withdrawal and no-case procedure
key_facts: Mrs Woods appealed against abatement notices served by Sevenoaks District Council after motorcycle scrambling events at White Rocks Farm caused noise nuisance.
The first notice hearing was aborted when the chairman recused himself; the council withdrew the first notice and served a second notice, leading to separate appeals.
Justices refused costs relating to the withdrawn first notice and dismissed the second appeal after declining a no-case submission when the appellant had not yet opened her case.
The High Court on case stated considered whether council withdrawal terminated pending appeals and whether no-case procedure applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' court decisions on Environmental Protection Act abatement notice appeals.
enrichment.outcome: First notice quashed for limited purpose; both appeals otherwise dismissed; respondent's costs ordered; no jurisdiction to grant leave to appeal further.
enrichment.ratio: Withdrawal of an abatement notice cannot deprive magistrates of jurisdiction over a complaint already properly brought; where parties reverse the usual order of evidence by having the respondent open first, an appellant wishing to make no-case submissions must elect not to call evidence; costs refusals were within the justices' wide discretion given linked proceedings.
legal_issues: Effect of local authority withdrawal of an abatement notice on pending appeals
Whether magistrates should have quashed the first notice and awarded costs
Propriety of refusing a no-case submission before the appellant's evidence
Whether the second appeal decision was perverse on the evidence

notes: Patent revocation action on school radio attendance system; claims 1-2 invalid, claim 7 valid.

enrichment.short_title: School radio attendance patent: claims 1 and 2 revoked for obviousness
key_facts: The Secretary of State sought revocation of European patent (UK) No 0664061 owned by Frontline Technology Ltd for an attendance registration system by radio link.
The patent related to electronic school pupil registration using radio-linked terminals after computerised attendance records were permitted.
Validity of independent claims 1, 2 and 7 was contested, with priority and prior use issues involving associated company Bromcom Computers' school installations.
Kingshurst prior use rendered claims 1 and 2 obvious, but claim 7 survived attacks based on prior art and intervening use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patent revocation action in the Patents Court concerning selected independent claims.
enrichment.outcome: Claims 1 and 2 found obvious and lacking inventive step; claim 7 held not obvious and valid.
enrichment.ratio: Claims 1 and 2 of the attendance registration patent lacked inventive step over the Kingshurst prior use system; the more advanced buffered RF protocol features of claim 7 were not anticipated or rendered obvious by Bromcom's earlier dumb RTU installations or intervening publications.
legal_issues: Obviousness of claims 1 and 2 over Kingshurst prior use
Validity and priority of claims 1, 2 and 7
Whether Bromcom school deployments anticipated or made obvious claim 7
Confidentiality and enablement of prior use evidence

notes: Pharmaceutical parallel import reference; Court of Appeal settled ECJ questions on reboxing and overstickering.

enrichment.short_title: ECJ reference on parallel import reboxing and overstickering conditions
key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal judgment of 5 March 2004 in Boehringer Ingelheim v Swingward, parties failed to agree questions for an ECJ reference and submitted rival sets.
The dispute concerns parallel import of pharmaceutical products by reboxing or overstickering and compliance with Bristol-Myers Squibb v Paranova conditions.
Issues include burden of proof, necessity of repackaging, reputation damage from de-branding or co-branding, and remedies for failure to give notice.
Jacob LJ formulated consolidated questions for referral covering reboxed products, overstickered products, and notice failures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judgment settling questions to be referred to the ECJ after prior appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Questions referred to the ECJ as formulated by the court; appeals adjourned pending ECJ answers; no order for interim costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties cannot agree ECJ questions after a trade mark reference is required, the court should formulate its own questions, erring on inclusion and basing them on the defendants' draft while incorporating claimants' points; costs of the reference stage should await the ECJ outcome in large multi-issue litigation.
legal_issues: Burden of proof on Paranova conditions for reboxed and overstickered pharmaceuticals
Whether necessity condition applies to manner of reboxing or overstickering
Scope of the reputation-damage condition including de-branding and co-branding
Remedies and proportionality where notice requirements are breached

notes: Welsh-medium school transport JR; Collins J quashed refusal where nearer English school unsuitable.

enrichment.short_title: Free school transport to Welsh-medium school beyond walking distance
key_facts: Three Ceredigion children attended Welsh-medium Ysgol Preseli in Pembrokeshire by parental preference, about 8 miles from home.
The nearest secondary school Cardigan was within statutory walking distance but English-medium and accepted as unsuitable; Dyffryn Teifi was suitable Welsh-medium but about 18 miles away.
Ceredigion refused free transport to Preseli, expecting attendance at Dyffryn Teifi; the transport appeal panel upheld that decision.
Pembrokeshire ceased funding cross-border spare seats unless Ceredigion paid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a home-to-school transport appeal panel decision.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; panel decision quashed; local authority required to provide free transport to Preseli as nearest suitable school.
enrichment.ratio: A local education authority must provide necessary free transport under section 509 where parents would have a section 444(4) defence to truancy prosecution; suitable arrangements under section 444(4)(b)(iii) cannot rely on registering a child at a nearer school that is educationally unsuitable, and an authority cannot rationally treat an unsuitable nearer school as displacing the transport duty.
legal_issues: Link between section 509 transport duty and section 444 truancy defences
Whether suitability in section 444(4)(b)(iii) governs arrangements or the nearer school
Proper test of school suitability for transport purposes
Effect of parental preference for a nearer suitable Welsh-medium school in another authority
